1	# wiki-growth worker
2	
3	One compile-once/refine-in-place research pass over the repo's product wikis (the Karpathy LLM-wiki pattern):
4	read what the wiki already knows, research only what its own backlog flags, write it back cited. **Most runs
5	find little or nothing — no new citable material means no branch, no PR, and that is the documented good
6	outcome.** A padded or fabricated update is worse than none.
7	
8	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue; GitHub access is the session's
9	**GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`) — never `gh`/`curl`/a clone. "Default branch" below means the repo's
10	actual default branch. The wiki set is derived **structurally**: every `README.md` at depth ≥ 2 under
11	`product-wiki/`, excluding the `product-wiki/product-requirements/` and `product-wiki/sample-data/` subtrees.
12	
13	The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: it may open a PR but never merges one and never pushes to
14	the default branch.
15	
16	## Preflight
17	
18	**Before researching**, search the repo for an open PR whose head branch matches `claude/product-wiki-growth/*`.
19	If one is open, do **not** stack a second round of unreviewed research on it — add one dated nudge comment on
20	that PR and stop.
21	
22	This is the *only* guard against that stacking — nothing upstream covers it. The scheduler's at-most-one-open
23	guard is about **dispatch issues**, not pull requests: a completed run converges and closes its own dispatch
24	issue while leaving this task's PR open for the owner to review, so the next weekly slot sees an empty issue
25	family and dispatches normally. Expect to find an open growth PR whenever the last one hasn't been reviewed
26	yet; that is the ordinary case this preflight exists for, not an anomaly.
27	
28	## Method
29	
30	1. **Read every wiki page end to end** (`get_file_contents`), the `## Open questions` and `## Growth log`
31	   sections first-class. Never re-derive a claim that is already cited and current.
32	2. **Pick the one or two open questions** across the set most worth this run; also spot-check one or two
33	   existing citations for staleness (a dead link, a superseded stat). If the Context flagged a product-wiki
34	   change in the window, spot-check the pages it may have superseded.
35	3. **Research.** *Web mode* (WebSearch/WebFetch available): the open web. *Repo-derived mode* (web tools
36	   absent — do not fail, do not fake): citable repo-native signal only — new feature-request/extractor-request
37	   issues, merged PRs, issue/PR discussion carrying user-side signal — each citable to its own GitHub URL.
38	4. **Write into the relevant wiki page(s) only**, per the pack's RULES.md: cite every claim in that page's
39	   `## Sources`; correct a wrong or superseded claim with a note of why, never a silent deletion; touch
40	   `product-wiki/sample-data/` only when a new claim needs an illustrative example; **never write
41	   `product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — a finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note
42	   (and a repo issue) and waits for a human.
43	5. **Reconcile the page's `## Key insights` header** with what the body now says. It leads the page, it is
44	   bullets only, and it is capped (seven bullets, 140 characters each — about one line) — so a new insight
45	   that belongs at the top usually displaces a weaker one rather than being appended. Each bullet is one
46	   finding in plain words: no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, and preferably something a reader
47	   who knows the field would *not* already assume. Judging obviousness is hard, so when in doubt keep the
48	   line rather than agonising — short and slightly obvious beats long and careful. Rewrite a bullet the run
49	   superseded (the correction and its *why* live in the body, not in the header); leave the header alone
50	   when the run changed nothing about the page's top-line understanding. **Never restate the header as a
51	   table of contents** — each bullet is a finding a reader can act on.
52	6. **One dated `## Growth log` entry per touched page** (`- **YYYY-MM-DD** — what changed`).
53	7. **Update `## Open questions` both directions** — remove what this run answered, add what its research
54	   surfaced.
55	
56	## Stop condition
57	
58	Neither mode yields citable material → stop. No commit, no log entry, no PR.
59	
60	## Delivery
61	
62	Branch `claude/product-wiki-growth/<date>` (unique branch per run), commits touching only `product-wiki/**`
63	minus `product-requirements/`, one **PR — never merged, never pushed to the default branch directly**.
64	Web-researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate. PR body: the question(s)
65	researched, what changed where, the citations added, and the open questions left for the next run.
66	
67	## Tracking
68	
69	Standing issue found by exact title **"Claudinite tracker: Product Wiki Growth"** in the repo — found by
70	title, never by number, never opened/closed as state (open it if missing). One dated comment when a pass
71	**grew** (`grew (PR #N): <one line>`) or was **blocked** (`blocked: <why>` — the human-visible convergence for

# wiki-growth worker

One compile-once/refine-in-place research pass over the repo's product wikis (the Karpathy LLM-wiki pattern):
read what the wiki already knows, research only what its own backlog flags, write it back cited. **Most runs
find little or nothing — no new citable material means no branch, no PR, and that is the documented good
outcome.** A padded or fabricated update is worse than none.

You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue; GitHub access is the session's
**GitHub MCP tools** (`mcp__github__*`) — never `gh`/`curl`/a clone. "Default branch" below means the repo's
actual default branch. The wiki set is derived **structurally**: every `README.md` at depth ≥ 2 under
`product-wiki/`, excluding the `product-wiki/product-requirements/` and `product-wiki/sample-data/` subtrees.

The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: it may open a PR but never merges one and never pushes to
the default branch.

## Preflight

**Before researching**, search the repo for an open PR whose head branch matches `claude/product-wiki-growth/*`.
If one is open, do **not** stack a second round of unreviewed research on it — add one dated nudge comment on
that PR and stop.

This is the *only* guard against that stacking — nothing upstream covers it. The scheduler's at-most-one-open
guard is about **dispatch issues**, not pull requests: a completed run converges and closes its own dispatch
issue while leaving this task's PR open for the owner to review, so the next weekly slot sees an empty issue
family and dispatches normally. Expect to find an open growth PR whenever the last one hasn't been reviewed
yet; that is the ordinary case this preflight exists for, not an anomaly.

## Method

1. **Read every wiki page end to end** (`get_file_contents`), the `## Open questions` and `## Growth log`
   sections first-class. Never re-derive a claim that is already cited and current.
2. **Pick the one or two open questions** across the set most worth this run; also spot-check one or two
   existing citations for staleness (a dead link, a superseded stat). If the Context flagged a product-wiki
   change in the window, spot-check the pages it may have superseded.
3. **Research.** *Web mode* (WebSearch/WebFetch available): the open web. *Repo-derived mode* (web tools
   absent — do not fail, do not fake): citable repo-native signal only — new feature-request/extractor-request
   issues, merged PRs, issue/PR discussion carrying user-side signal — each citable to its own GitHub URL.
4. **Write into the relevant wiki page(s) only**, per the pack's RULES.md: cite every claim in that page's
   `## Sources`; correct a wrong or superseded claim with a note of why, never a silent deletion; touch
   `product-wiki/sample-data/` only when a new claim needs an illustrative example; **never write
   `product-wiki/product-requirements/`** — a finding that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note
   (and a repo issue) and waits for a human.
5. **Reconcile the page's `## Key insights` header** with what the body now says. It leads the page, it is
   bullets only, and it is capped (seven bullets, 140 characters each — about one line) — so a new insight
   that belongs at the top usually displaces a weaker one rather than being appended. Each bullet is one
   finding in plain words: no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, and preferably something a reader
   who knows the field would *not* already assume. Judging obviousness is hard, so when in doubt keep the
   line rather than agonising — short and slightly obvious beats long and careful. Rewrite a bullet the run
   superseded (the correction and its *why* live in the body, not in the header); leave the header alone
   when the run changed nothing about the page's top-line understanding. **Never restate the header as a
   table of contents** — each bullet is a finding a reader can act on.
6. **One dated `## Growth log` entry per touched page** (`- **YYYY-MM-DD** — what changed`).
7. **Update `## Open questions` both directions** — remove what this run answered, add what its research
   surfaced.

## Stop condition

Neither mode yields citable material → stop. No commit, no log entry, no PR.

## Delivery

Branch `claude/product-wiki-growth/<date>` (unique branch per run), commits touching only `product-wiki/**`
minus `product-requirements/`, one **PR — never merged, never pushed to the default branch directly**.

researched, what changed where, the citations added, and the open questions left for the next run.

title, never by number, never opened/closed as state (open it if missing). One dated comment when a pass
**grew** (`grew (PR #N): <one line>`) or was **blocked** (`blocked: <why>` — the human-visible convergence for
a failed unattended run). Clean no-ops stay silent — the pack's freshness advisory is the prolonged-silence
observer.

fabrication.

Edit `product-wiki/product-requirements/`; edit anything outside `product-wiki/`; create new wiki folders

claim without a superseded note; leave a `## Key insights` header asserting what the body it heads no longer
says; pad a growth log, a header, or a wiki page to look productive; merge or approve its own
PR; schedule anything (no cron, no `schedule:` workflow); touch the shared canon.

# product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki

This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki
under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in
place). Layout, required page sections, the Key insights header's shape,
growth-log dating, source links, staleness, and the isolation wall are
**check-enforced** — the finding is the instruction, so this prose never restates
them. The full growth procedure is the pack's task doc
(`packs/product-wiki/tasks/wiki-growth/task.md`).

- **Every page opens with what it found.** `## Key insights` leads the page: a
  few bullets carrying the research's actual conclusions — the numbers, the
  competitor that already does this, the thing that turned out not to be true —
  enough that a human who reads only the header understands what was researched
  and what it means. Not a table of contents ("covers pricing and competitors"),
  not a teaser. The body is where the reader goes for evidence, nuance and
  citations; the header is where they decide whether they need to.
- **Terse, plain, and only the non-obvious.** One short line per bullet, in
  ordinary words — no qualifying clause, no citation, no hedge, no jargon a
  newcomer would have to decode. Prefer the finding that would *surprise*
  someone who knows the field: the thing that turned out not to be true, the
  number nobody expects, the competitor who already shipped it. Whether a point
  is obvious is genuinely hard to call, so **don't agonise — when in doubt, keep
  it**. A borderline-obvious line costs the reader two seconds; a long, careful
  line costs them the header.
- **The header is a current view, not a log.** A pass that changes what a page's
  most important findings are rewrites the header to match — a superseded
  insight leaves it (the correction and its why stay in the body, per below),
  and an insight the pass didn't touch stays put. If nothing changed the page's
  top-line understanding, the header doesn't move.
- **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never
  changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding
  that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and
  waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
  build on.
- **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before
  researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as
  open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass.
  Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current.
- **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A
  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source),
  never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's
  growth log and updates the open questions in both directions.
- **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable
  material → no edit, no log entry, no PR.
- **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when
  a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test
  asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/`
  outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so
  create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation
  refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
- **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR —
  researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate.
  The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method
  in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline.

1	# Competitors
2	
3	A self-growing survey of tools competing to do what this extension does: get an
4	event from a webpage onto a calendar with minimal friction. Not exhaustive — a
5	general lay of the land, kept current by the Claudinite **product-wiki** pack's
6	growth worker (mounted read-only under `.claudinite/`).
7	Sibling to [`../Market/`](../Market/README.md) (the calendar-market
8	landscape) and [`../Users/`](../Users/README.md) (who uses this
9	extension).
10	
11	## Landscape (as of 2026-07-15)
12	
13	| Tool | Approach | Notes |
14	|---|---|---|
15	| [Eventy](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/eventy/kfancgcbhdkeohknmidbnioccmmoknjl) | AI extraction from webpages, email, flyers, concert posters, even screenshots | Broadest input surface of the group; 4.4★ on the Chrome Web Store. Exports to Google Calendar or `.ics` (Outlook/Apple Calendar) — covers the multi-calendar gap this project doesn't (see Market open question). |
16	| [Add To Calendar](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/add-to-calendar/jnbpajadakhkpcncmbfhkgaaoioofkfd) | Highlight text → right-click → "Intelligent Technology" scan for title/date/time/address | 4.4★. Closest in spirit to a lightweight, single-purpose tool rather than a broad AI product. |
17	| [Calendar Event Creator](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/calendar-event-creator/nbdaijdcnmhjhoekcdcgdjcjheajgpad) | Select event text → right-click → OpenAI API extracts details | Requires an OpenAI-backed flow — a real friction point vs. "no API key" positioning. |
18	| [ChatGPT for Google Calendar](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/chatgpt-for-google-calend/laejdmahdkleahgkdpiapfdcmleedhca) | LLM-based extraction of title/date/time/location from any webpage | Google-Calendar-only, like this project, but LLM-dependent rather than rule-based + generic-fallback. |
19	| [Smart Calendars AI](https://www.smartcalendars.ai/en/articles/browser-extension-add-events) | "Turns what you're reading into ready-to-review calendar events" | Cross-browser (Chrome + Safari) — worth tracking if Safari support ever becomes relevant here. |
20	| [CalendarAdd](https://github.com/mattkrins/CalendarAdd) | Open-source Chrome extension: select text → Google Calendar event | Same "no server, no account" spirit as this project, but text-selection-only (no per-site structured extraction, no JSON-LD awareness). |
21	| Axiom.ai / Bardeen | General no-code browser-automation platforms; calendar event creation is one of many workflows, not a dedicated product | Not direct competitors for a casual user, but relevant if "add to calendar" ever gets framed as one automation among many rather than a single-purpose tool. |
22	
23	## Positioning takeaways
24	
25	- **Most competitors lean on a cloud AI/LLM API** (OpenAI or similar) for
26	  extraction, which typically means an account, a subscription, or at least a
27	  network call to a third party with the page's content. This project's
28	  rule-based per-site extractors + generic fallback (no OAuth, no API key, no
29	  content leaves the browser) is a real, defensible differentiator — worth
30	  stating explicitly in messaging/store listing copy, not just an implementation
31	  detail.
32	- **Multi-calendar export (`.ics`, Outlook, Apple Calendar) is common among
33	  AI-based competitors** (Eventy, Smart Calendars AI) but absent here — flagged
34	  as an open question in Market, now cross-referenced from the competitive
35	  angle too.
36	- **Ratings cluster around 4.4★** for the dedicated single-purpose tools — no
37	  major quality outlier found yet in this pass; revisit once review counts are
38	  gathered (not captured in this seed).
39	- **Cross-browser, the field is thinner and still selection-based.** Beyond the
40	  Chrome Web Store, Firefox carries "Create a Google Calendar Event" and "Checker
41	  Plus for Google Calendar" (highlight text → right-click → event), and
42	  Calendly / Smart Calendars AI span Chrome/Firefox/Edge/Safari — but these are
43	  right-click-selection or scheduling tools, not per-site structured extractors.
44	  No JSON-LD/microdata-aware competitor surfaced on Firefox/Edge either, so the
45	  structured-extraction niche is open cross-browser too, not just on Chrome.
46	- **The structured-extraction lane was occupied once, at microformat scale, and
47	  then vacated (checked 2026-07-26).** This sharpens the standing "still none
48	  found" answer into something more useful than absence. The closest thing that
49	  ever shipped was the **"Google Calendar" Chrome extension** — a hackathon
50	  project *"encouraged by the Chrome and Calendar teams at Google"*, since
51	  open-sourced and archived — which detected events on the page you were reading
52	  via the **`hCalendar` microformat and derivative microformats** and offered a
53	  one-click add. It is now **shut down**: the repo states *"This Chrome extension
54	  is no longer available to install, though the source code is available here to
55	  fork & modify"*, and the author's shutdown note cites request load from Google
56	  teams outweighing his available time, not lack of demand — the extension had
57	  **5MM+ users** at shutdown. The generic **"Microformats"** extension (exported
58	  `hCalendar` → iCalendar / add to Google Calendar) is likewise reported delisted
59	  and unmaintained since ~2014. Two readings, both worth carrying: the lane is
60	  genuinely empty *today*, and its last occupant died of maintenance cost at
61	  scale — the exact cost a rule-based per-site extractor set also accrues.
62	- **Structured-data awareness and calendar creation are disjoint categories in
63	  today's extension ecosystem.** JSON-LD-aware extensions are easy to find and
64	  effectively commoditised — **JSON-LD Schema Extractor** (Chrome *and* Firefox),
65	  **LD+JSON Extractor**, **JSON-LD Checker**, **SEO Schema Visualizer** — but every
66	  one is an SEO/developer *inspection* tool: extract, pretty-print, validate, or
67	  graph a page's structured data against schema.org. None turns an `Event` block
68	  into a calendar entry. So the answer to "is anyone doing per-site structured
69	  extraction?" is not that the capability is hard or rare — it is that nobody has
70	  wired the commodity parsing side to the calendar side. That junction is
71	  precisely this project's lane. (Caveat, same as the Safari findings: the store
72	  listings themselves return HTTP 403 to this worker's fetcher, so these rest on
73	  search-surfaced listing descriptions; the two GitHub sources below were read
74	  end to end.)
75	- **Safari, checked 2026-07-26, does not differ — and if anything leans further
76	  from structured extraction.** Three layers, none of them a per-site markup
77	  reader: (1) *browser extensions* — Smart Calendars AI is the one genuine
78	  event-capture extension spanning Chrome and Safari, and its own description
79	  puts it on **text and image recognition** plus select-text-on-a-page capture,
80	  never schema.org/JSON-LD; Calendly ships a Safari extension through the Mac App
81	  Store, but it is a scheduling-link tool, not an extractor. (2) *Standalone App
82	  Store apps taking the image route* — EventShot (Image To Calendar) and
83	  Screenshots to Calendar both turn a **screenshot** into an event (title, date,
84	  time, location; the latter also claims recurring-event and
85	  multiple-events-per-image detection). (3) *Apple's own OS-level path* is **Data
86	  Detectors**, which recognises dates in text and offers to create a Calendar
87	  event — but Apple documents it for Mac document apps (Mail, TextEdit, Preview),
88	  not as a Safari webpage-markup feature. So the structured-extraction niche is
89	  open on Safari too, and the Safari-native centre of gravity is OCR/text
90	  detection — the opposite end of the ladder from JSON-LD.
91	- **Screenshot/OCR capture is emerging as a distinct input axis.** Eventy already
92	  advertised flyer/poster/screenshot input; the Safari scan turned up two more
93	  image-first tools. This project has no answer to it by design — it reads the
94	  page's markup, and a screenshot has none — but the two approaches fail on
95	  opposite inputs, so this is a positioning question rather than a feature gap.

130	  fetches of the App Store and vendor listings, so the Safari findings rest on
131	  search-result summaries of those listings rather than the listings read end to
132	  end. A pass with a working fetcher should confirm the two image-first apps.
133	- Does the image/screenshot input axis (Eventy, EventShot, Screenshots to
134	  Calendar) draw users this project would otherwise reach, or is it serving a
135	  genuinely different moment — a photographed poster, not a page you're reading?
136	  Surfaced 2026-07-26.

1	# Domain
2	
3	A self-growing wiki of the **problem domain** this extension models: how events
4	are represented on the web, and how those representations shape what the
5	extension can extract. Where [`../Market/`](../Market/README.md),
6	[`../Users/`](../Users/README.md), and
7	[`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md) cover the outside actors (the
8	platforms, the people, the rivals), this wiki covers the *thing itself* — the
9	event data, formats, and page shapes the extractor has to make sense of. It is
10	the knowledge that most directly drives extraction requirements.
11	
12	## Machine-readable event formats (as of 2026-07-16)
13	
14	Ordered roughly by how useful they are to a rule-based extractor — highest-signal
15	first. The project's stance (see the **architecture rules of the road** section of
16	`.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/RULES.md`, where it reads "prefer extracting
17	JSON-LD/`og:` (which apps still inject) over brittle DOM positions" — the
18	`dev/procedures/technicalGotchas.md` this page previously cited was superseded
19	when that doc was folded into the gcec pack) is to **prefer machine-readable
20	markup over brittle DOM scraping**, because it survives redesigns and
21	single-page-app rendering.
22	
23	- **schema.org `Event` as JSON-LD** — the highest-value target and the one Google
24	  actively rewards. Emitted as a standalone `<script type="application/ld+json">`
25	  block, so it is cleanly separable from the page markup and survives client-side
26	  rendering. Google's required properties are **`name`, `startDate`, and
27	  `location`**; `startDate`/`endDate` are ISO-8601 **with a UTC/GMT offset**
28	  (the offset is what lets us derive `ctz` safely — see
29	  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js`).
30	  `location` is a `Place` (with `address`: `streetAddress`, `addressLocality`,
31	  `addressRegion`, `postalCode`) or a `VirtualLocation` (URL only) for online
32	  events. Since 2020 Google also expects **`eventAttendanceMode`**
33	  (`Offline`/`Online`/`Mixed`), and as of a June 2025 change requires a **physical
34	  location** for the rich result at all. Recommended extras that often carry real
35	  data: `endDate`, `eventStatus`, `image`, `description`, `offers`.
36	- **Microdata / RDFa** (schema.org vocabulary inline in the HTML) — same
37	  vocabulary, embedded in the markup rather than a separate block. Common on
38	  server-rendered sites; JSON-LD is now preferred and gets new features first, so
39	  microdata/RDFa are a declining but still-present fallback worth reading when no
40	  JSON-LD block exists. Web-wide, Microdata is still material — the *Web Almanac
41	  2024* has it steady on roughly a quarter of pages (~26%), well ahead of
42	  microformats below.
43	- **`h-event` / hCalendar microformats** — an older, class-attribute convention
44	  (`h-event`, `p-name`, `dt-start`, `p-location`). Google added hCalendar event
45	  support back in 2010; adoption has been overtaken by schema.org, but legacy and
46	  indie-web event pages still use it. **A 2026 prevalence check settles whether
47	  they're worth a dedicated reader — no:** the HTTP Archive *Web Almanac 2024*
48	  puts *all* microformats combined below ~1% of pages (hCalendar only a fraction
49	  of that), against JSON-LD at ~41% (up from 34% in 2022) and Microdata steady at
50	  ~26%. So `h-event`/hCalendar is a negligible tail; where it does appear, the
51	  generic text/`og:` fallback is enough. Note: microformats are **not** part of
52	  the schema.org vocabulary, so any dedicated reader would need its own parser —
53	  another reason not to build one for a sub-1% format. **Tooling corroboration
54	  (2026-07-26):** the one browser tool that ever shipped a microformat→calendar
55	  reader at scale — the Google-encouraged "Google Calendar" Chrome extension,
56	  which detected `hCalendar` and derivative microformats on the page and offered
57	  a one-click add — is formally shut down and no longer installable, and the
58	  generic "Microformats" extension that exported `hCalendar` to iCalendar is
59	  likewise reported delisted (unmaintained since ~2014). So there is also no
60	  live microformat event reader left to borrow from (the demand-side reading of
61	  the same fact is in [`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md)).
62	- **OpenGraph / meta tags** (`og:title`, `og:description`, and event-ish `<meta>`)
63	  — not event-specific, but SPA pages very often still inject them, so they are a
64	  reliable low-fidelity fallback for title/description when nothing structured
65	  exists.
66	- **iCalendar (`.ics` / RFC 5545)** — the interchange format calendars import,
67	  not usually embedded in a page, but the semantic reference for event modelling.
68	  A `VEVENT` carries `DTSTART`/`DTEND` with a **`TZID`** (or a trailing `Z` for
69	  UTC, or a bare **floating** time that means "the same wall-clock time in every
70	  zone"). Recurrence is an **`RRULE`** (`FREQ` = DAILY/WEEKLY/MONTHLY/YEARLY plus
71	  `INTERVAL`/`COUNT`/`UNTIL`/`BYDAY`…) expanded from `DTSTART`, with `RDATE`/`EXDATE`
72	  adjustments. This is the vocabulary to match when we reason about timezones and
73	  repeats even though we target Google Calendar's `render` URL, not `.ics`.
74	
75	## Page-shape taxonomy
76	
77	The extractor must first recognise *what kind of event page* it's on — this is the
78	structural decision behind "one button per event":
79	
80	- **Single-event page** — one clear event (a concert, a talk, a venue listing).
81	  Usually one `Event` JSON-LD block or one hero heading + date/venue. The common
82	  case.
83	- **Listing / index page** — a calendar-of-events or search-results page with many
84	  entries, often an array of `Event` objects or repeated cards. Drives the
85	  multiple-buttons behaviour; the generic fallback can't reliably enumerate these
86	  (it recovers the primary event only — see the fallback-coverage gate).
87	- **Series / recurring page** — one event described as repeating (an `RRULE` in
88	  `.ics`, or schema.org `eventSchedule`). A single page can imply many instances;
89	  how many to surface is genuinely undecided (see Open questions).
90	
91	## Timezone & recurrence semantics
92	
93	- **Timezone** is the trust-critical field: a wrong `ctz` is worse than none —
94	  the unanimity rule, stated in the contract header of
95	  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js` itself (not in the gcec
96	  pack's RULES.md): a zone is returned **only when two independent page-declared
97	  hints agree**, and `""` whenever anything disagrees. The four hint kinds that
98	  file recognises are *stated* (an IANA zone in inline-script JSON), *offset* (the
99	  event's own UTC offset — a trailing `Z` explicitly does **not** count, since
100	  pages habitually serialize in UTC regardless of venue), *country*, and *locale*.
101	  The domain gives three shapes — an
102	  **offset-bearing** instant (ISO-8601 `…+02:00`, or `.ics` `Z`/`TZID`), a
103	  **floating** time (no zone; "same wall-clock everywhere"), and **no time signal
104	  at all**. Only the first lets `ctz` be *derived* rather than guessed.
105	- **Recurrence** (`RRULE`, `eventSchedule`) is currently out of the extension's
106	  scope — it surfaces the event, not its repeat rule. Whether a recurring page
107	  should yield one instance, the next instance, or a note is an open product
108	  question, not a settled requirement. Two 2026 findings narrow *where* the cost
109	  of ever changing that sits:
110	  - **The sink is not the blocker.** Google Calendar's
111	    `render?action=TEMPLATE` link — the exact URL this extension emits — takes an
112	    optional **`recur`** parameter whose value is an RFC-5545 recurrence rule
113	    verbatim: `recur=RRULE:FREQ=DAILY` (`required: no`, `format: text
114	    (RFC-5545 specs)`), and in practice fuller rules such as
115	    `recur=RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;INTERVAL=1;BYDAY=2MO;UNTIL=20250609T000000Z`. So
116	    "hand the user a repeating event" is already expressible in the target we
117	    emit; nothing about the render URL forces the one-instance behaviour.
118	  - **The source side speaks a different vocabulary.** schema.org does *not*
119	    express repeats as an `RRULE` string. A repeating event carries
120	    **`eventSchedule`** → a **`Schedule`**, whose minimum is **`repeatFrequency`
121	    as an ISO-8601 *duration*** (`P1W`, `P1M`, `P1D` — not `FREQ=WEEKLY`),
122	    alongside `byDay` / `byMonth` / `byMonthDay` (e.g. `byDay` as an array of
123	    `https://schema.org/Monday`-style URLs), `scheduleTimezone` (an IANA zone),
124	    `startDate`/`endDate`, `startTime`/`endTime`, and `exceptDate` for
125	    exclusions. Emitting `recur=` from page markup therefore needs a genuine
126	    translation step (`repeatFrequency: P1W` + `byDay` → `FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=…`,
127	    `exceptDate` → `EXDATE`), not a pass-through. **That mapping — plus whether
128	    target sites emit `eventSchedule` at all — is the real cost, not the URL.**
129	
130	## Implications for extraction requirements
131	
132	- The format ranking above is *why* the extractor is structured as dedicated
133	  per-site sources + a generic JSON-LD/`og`-first fallback: the machine-readable
134	  layers are the durable signal, the DOM is the last resort.
135	- "An event needs real data, not just a supported host" (gcec pack RULES.md,
136	  *Codebase gotchas*) is a direct consequence of the taxonomy: a host match is
137	  not an `Event` object.
138	- The timezone shapes above are the domain justification for the refusal-to-guess
139	  `ctz` contract — a product-requirements-level stance, distilled in
140	  [`../product-requirements/`](../product-requirements/README.md).
141	- **`Event` JSON-LD is real but a minority signal.** The Google/schema.org usage
142	  statistics (June 2026 dataset) put `schema.org/Event` on **fewer than ~1 million
143	  domains** — an order of magnitude behind common types like `author` (10M+);
144	  Web Data Commons corroborates from the Common Crawl corpus. So a large share of
145	  event pages carry *no* `Event` block, which is exactly why the DOM/text and
146	  `og:`/microdata fallback path (and the fallback-coverage routine) carries real
147	  weight rather than being a rare edge case.
148	- **No dedicated microformats reader is warranted.** The 2026 prevalence check
149	  (see the `h-event` bullet) puts *all* microformats combined under ~1% of pages,
150	  so `h-event`/hCalendar stays a fallback-only concern — extraction effort belongs
151	  on the JSON-LD → Microdata → `og:`/text ladder, not a bespoke hCalendar parser.
152

157	  a measured split over the sites this extension actually sees; the
158	  fallback-coverage corpus is the place to derive that.

164	- Do any of this extension's target sites actually emit `eventSchedule` /

2	
3	A self-growing wiki of the market environment this extension operates in: what
4	calendar platforms exist, what kinds of pages people extract events from, and
5	what usage patterns show up in that market. Distinct from
6	[`../Users/`](../Users/README.md) (who uses *this* extension and how) and
7	[`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md) (who else builds this).
8	
9	## How this wiki grows
10	
11	This follows Andrej Karpathy's ["LLM Wiki" pattern](https://medium.com/@urvvil08/andrej-karpathys-llm-wiki-create-your-own-knowledge-base-8779014accd5):
12	instead of re-deriving market context from scratch on every question, an agent
13	**compiles** findings into this file once and **refines it in place** on later
14	passes — later runs read what's already here before researching, extend or
15	correct it, cite every claim, and only prune a claim when it's superseded (never
16	silently). The mechanic (schedule, what counts as a real update, when to open a
17	PR) is owned by the Claudinite **product-wiki** pack's growth worker (mounted
18	read-only under `.claudinite/`).
19	Nothing in this file is guaranteed current — check the growth log's date and
20	treat older entries as a starting point to verify, not ground truth.
21	
22	## Calendar platform landscape (as of 2026-07-15)
23	
24	- The calendar-app market was valued around **$14.6B in 2025**, projected to grow
25	  at roughly **10.8% CAGR through 2034**.
26	- **Google, Microsoft, and Apple** are the dominant players; Google Calendar and
27	  web Outlook together account for the majority of web-based platform usage.
28	  Google Calendar alone is reported in use at **637,000+ companies** in 2026 (62.6%
29	  US-based).
30	- **Web-based platforms held the largest share (38.2% in 2025)** of the calendar
31	  app market, ahead of native mobile/desktop apps — consistent with this
32	  extension's approach (a browser action, not a native app).
33	- Google Calendar's event-creation URL scheme
34	  (`calendar.google.com/calendar/render?action=TEMPLATE`) — what this extension
35	  targets — has no first-party equivalent this project currently uses for Outlook
36	  or Apple Calendar. Google Calendar is ~23% of the calendar-tool market (6sense),
37	  but the portable multi-calendar path is **`.ics` (RFC 5545)**, not per-vendor
38	  deep links: Outlook, Apple Calendar, and any RFC-5545 app both export and import
39	  it, and existing Chrome extensions (ics2gcal, ICS to GCal) already one-click a
40	  `.ics` into Google Calendar. So the export question is really "emit a standards
41	  `.ics`" rather than "add an Outlook deep link" — the same lever the AI
42	  competitors already pull (Eventy, Smart Calendars AI; see Competitors). Tradeoff:
43	  a `.ics` is a *download*, where the render URL is a no-download click-through —
44	  the exact friction this product optimises away.
45	
46	## Event-source landscape (what pages people extract *from*)
47	
48	Sites the extension already has dedicated extractors for (see
49	`extension/event-extractors/custom/` and `dev/requirements/extractor/`) are
50	themselves representative of the market: ticketing/listing platforms (e.g.
51	Meetup, Ticketmaster) and single-venue/organizer sites. Two broad source shapes
52	recur across the market:
53	
54	- **Single-event pages** — a venue, a talk, a concert; one clear event, often with
55	  `schema.org`/JSON-LD event markup (the highest-signal, most future-proof
56	  extraction target — see the JSON-LD note in the **architecture rules of the
57	  road** section of `.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/RULES.md`; the
58	  `technicalGotchas.md` this line previously cited was superseded when that doc
59	  was folded into the gcec pack).
60	  Machine-readable markup is increasingly common because search engines reward it
61	  (Google's "Events" rich results), which is a structural tailwind for any
62	  extension that prefers JSON-LD/`og:` over brittle DOM scraping — but "common" is
63	  a *page-wide* fact, not an event-specific one, and this line overstated it until
64	  2026-07-26: JSON-LD reaches ~41% of pages and Microdata ~26%, while
65	  `schema.org/Event` specifically is on fewer than ~1M domains. The tailwind is
66	  real; it does not mean most event pages are structured. See
67	  [`../Domain/`](../Domain/README.md)'s format ranking.
68	- **Listing/series pages** — a calendar-of-events page with several entries; the
69	  extension already special-cases "one button per event" for this shape (see
70	  `product-requirements/README.md` requirement 4).
71	
72	## Usage patterns / use cases
73	
74	- **One-off personal use** — someone reads about a concert/talk/meetup in a
75	  newsletter, blog post, or social share and wants it on their calendar
76	  immediately, without leaving the page or typing anything.
77	- **Event discovery browsing** — scanning a listing/aggregator page and adding
78	  several events from one visit.
79	- **Professional scheduling from a webpage** — a conference agenda, a webinar
80	  registration page, an internal event site.

16	## Personas (initial pass — refine as real usage signal appears)
17	
18	- **The one-click saver.** Reads about a single event (a concert, a talk, a
19	  meetup) somewhere on the web and wants it on their calendar before they forget,
20	  with the least possible friction — no typing, no new account, no app switch.
21	  This is the extension's primary target today (see `product-requirements/`
22	  requirement 1).
23	- **The event browser.** Lands on a listing/series page with several events and
24	  wants to cherry-pick a few — served by the "one button per event" requirement.
25	- **The privacy-conscious user.** Actively avoids extensions that want an OAuth
26	  grant, an account, or send page content to a third-party AI API just to copy a
27	  date into a calendar. This persona is who the "no sign-in, no API key" product
28	  requirement is *for* — see the positioning notes in
29	  [`../Competitors/README.md`](../Competitors/README.md). This concern is
30	  well-grounded, not niche: 2026 studies report **86% of the top-100 Chrome
31	  extensions request high-risk permissions at install**, **52% of AI-branded
32	  extensions collect user data** (~1 in 3 collecting PII), and **71% of extensions
33	  publish no privacy policy** — and Chrome grants permissions at install that
34	  persist across every future update. A rule-based, no-OAuth, no-API-key,
35	  nothing-leaves-the-browser design answers exactly this anxiety.
36	
37	## Usage patterns
38	
39	- Single click → review pre-filled Google Calendar event → save. The extension
40	  deliberately stops short of auto-saving, so the user always reviews before
41	  committing (see `dev/requirements/requirements.md`).
42	- Works from whatever page the user is already on — no search, no lookup, no
43	  separate "paste a URL" step, unlike several competitor tools (see
44	  `../Competitors/README.md`).

49	  fallback-coverage routine (`.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/fallback-extractor-improvements/`) is the

53	  unanimity rule in the contract header of

content.content:
# `user-submitted/` — hand-supplied fixture pages

Recorded fixture pages (`<name>.html` + `<name>.url`) that a **user or developer
supplied by hand**, rather than the auto-extractor pipeline fetching them via
ScraperAPI. The intended use is the case the pipeline can't cover itself: when the
CI datacenter is bot-blocked from a target site, a person pastes the page's HTML in
so the site can still get a reviewed integration case.

This folder is empty today — it exists to mark the convention for that future flow.

## Why a separate folder from `server-fetched/`

The split is by **provenance**, and it's structural on purpose. GitHub secret
scanning / push protection can only be scoped by **path** (`secret_scanning.yml`
has a single `paths-ignore` knob — no per-secret or per-source option), so the
trust boundary has to *be* the folder:

- [`../server-fetched/`](../server-fetched/) — pipeline-recorded third-party pages.
  Their only embedded tokens are the **site's own** (e.g. a Mapbox key in the
  markup), never ours or a user's, so `.github/secret_scanning.yml` excludes that
  folder from push protection (a block there only wedges the pipeline — see #286).
- **this folder** — hand-supplied HTML, which could carry a **real** secret, so it
  is **not** excluded: push protection stays on and will block an accidental one at
  push time.

The test suite resolves a case's page from **either** folder
(`dev/requirements/extractor/data-files.js`), so dropping a `<name>.{html,url}` pair
here (plus its `expected/<name>.json`) wires it into `live.test.js` with no other
change.

## Key insights

- Not one of the 36 recorded event pages emits schema.org `eventSchedule`, so the recurrence mapping cost is moot.
- `schema.org/Event` sits on under 1M domains, so most event pages carry no Event block at all.
- Of this project's own 24 recorded target hosts, 14 carry Event JSON-LD; the other 10 need DOM, `og:` or text.
- Microformats together are under 1% of pages, so `h-event` never justifies its own parser.
- Google Calendar's render URL already accepts `recur=RRULE:…` — repeats were never blocked by the link we emit.
- A wrong timezone beats no timezone nowhere: a zone ships only when two independent page hints agree.
- No recorded target page offers a `.ics` download in place of markup; that page shape does not appear.

1	# Domain
2	
3	A self-growing wiki of the **problem domain** this extension models: how events
4	are represented on the web, and how those representations shape what the
5	extension can extract. Where [`../Market/`](../Market/README.md),
6	[`../Users/`](../Users/README.md), and
7	[`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md) cover the outside actors (the
8	platforms, the people, the rivals), this wiki covers the *thing itself* — the
9	event data, formats, and page shapes the extractor has to make sense of. It is
10	the knowledge that most directly drives extraction requirements.
11	
12	## Key insights
13	
14	- Not one of the 36 recorded event pages emits schema.org `eventSchedule`, so the recurrence mapping cost is moot.
15	- `schema.org/Event` sits on under 1M domains, so most event pages carry no Event block at all.
16	- Of this project's own 24 recorded target hosts, 14 carry Event JSON-LD; the other 10 need DOM, `og:` or text.
17	- Microformats together are under 1% of pages, so `h-event` never justifies its own parser.
18	- Google Calendar's render URL already accepts `recur=RRULE:…` — repeats were never blocked by the link we emit.
19	- A wrong timezone is worse than none, so a zone ships only when two independent page hints agree.
20	- No recorded target page offers a `.ics` download in place of markup; that page shape does not appear.
21	
22	## Machine-readable event formats (as of 2026-07-16)
23	
24	Ordered roughly by how useful they are to a rule-based extractor — highest-signal
25	first. The project's stance (see the **architecture rules of the road** section of
26	`.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/RULES.md`, where it reads "prefer extracting
27	JSON-LD/`og:` (which apps still inject) over brittle DOM positions" — the
28	`dev/procedures/technicalGotchas.md` this page previously cited was superseded
29	when that doc was folded into the gcec pack) is to **prefer machine-readable
30	markup over brittle DOM scraping**, because it survives redesigns and
31	single-page-app rendering.
32	
33	- **schema.org `Event` as JSON-LD** — the highest-value target and the one Google
34	  actively rewards. Emitted as a standalone `<script type="application/ld+json">`
35	  block, so it is cleanly separable from the page markup and survives client-side
36	  rendering. Google's required properties are **`name`, `startDate`, and
37	  `location`**; `startDate`/`endDate` are ISO-8601 **with a UTC/GMT offset**
38	  (the offset is what lets us derive `ctz` safely — see
39	  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js`).
40	  `location` is a `Place` (with `address`: `streetAddress`, `addressLocality`,
41	  `addressRegion`, `postalCode`) or a `VirtualLocation` (URL only) for online
42	  events. Since 2020 Google also expects **`eventAttendanceMode`**
43	  (`Offline`/`Online`/`Mixed`), and as of a June 2025 change requires a **physical
44	  location** for the rich result at all. Recommended extras that often carry real
45	  data: `endDate`, `eventStatus`, `image`, `description`, `offers`.
46	- **Microdata / RDFa** (schema.org vocabulary inline in the HTML) — same
47	  vocabulary, embedded in the markup rather than a separate block. Common on
48	  server-rendered sites; JSON-LD is now preferred and gets new features first, so
49	  microdata/RDFa are a declining but still-present fallback worth reading when no
50	  JSON-LD block exists. Web-wide, Microdata is still material — the *Web Almanac
51	  2024* has it steady on roughly a quarter of pages (~26%), well ahead of
52	  microformats below.
53	- **`h-event` / hCalendar microformats** — an older, class-attribute convention
54	  (`h-event`, `p-name`, `dt-start`, `p-location`). Google added hCalendar event
55	  support back in 2010; adoption has been overtaken by schema.org, but legacy and
56	  indie-web event pages still use it. **A 2026 prevalence check settles whether
57	  they're worth a dedicated reader — no:** the HTTP Archive *Web Almanac 2024*
58	  puts *all* microformats combined below ~1% of pages (hCalendar only a fraction
59	  of that), against JSON-LD at ~41% (up from 34% in 2022) and Microdata steady at
60	  ~26%. So `h-event`/hCalendar is a negligible tail; where it does appear, the
61	  generic text/`og:` fallback is enough. Note: microformats are **not** part of
62	  the schema.org vocabulary, so any dedicated reader would need its own parser —
63	  another reason not to build one for a sub-1% format. **Tooling corroboration
64	  (2026-07-26):** the one browser tool that ever shipped a microformat→calendar
65	  reader at scale — the Google-encouraged "Google Calendar" Chrome extension,
66	  which detected `hCalendar` and derivative microformats on the page and offered
67	  a one-click add — is formally shut down and no longer installable, and the
68	  generic "Microformats" extension that exported `hCalendar` to iCalendar is
69	  likewise reported delisted (unmaintained since ~2014). So there is also no
70	  live microformat event reader left to borrow from (the demand-side reading of
71	  the same fact is in [`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md)).
72	- **OpenGraph / meta tags** (`og:title`, `og:description`, and event-ish `<meta>`)
73	  — not event-specific, but SPA pages very often still inject them, so they are a
74	  reliable low-fidelity fallback for title/description when nothing structured
75	  exists.
76	- **iCalendar (`.ics` / RFC 5545)** — the interchange format calendars import,
77	  not usually embedded in a page, but the semantic reference for event modelling.
78	  A `VEVENT` carries `DTSTART`/`DTEND` with a **`TZID`** (or a trailing `Z` for
79	  UTC, or a bare **floating** time that means "the same wall-clock time in every
80	  zone"). Recurrence is an **`RRULE`** (`FREQ` = DAILY/WEEKLY/MONTHLY/YEARLY plus
81	  `INTERVAL`/`COUNT`/`UNTIL`/`BYDAY`…) expanded from `DTSTART`, with `RDATE`/`EXDATE`
82	  adjustments. This is the vocabulary to match when we reason about timezones and
83	  repeats even though we target Google Calendar's `render` URL, not `.ics`.
84	
85	## Page-shape taxonomy
86	
87	The extractor must first recognise *what kind of event page* it's on — this is the
88	structural decision behind "one button per event":
89	
90	- **Single-event page** — one clear event (a concert, a talk, a venue listing).
91	  Usually one `Event` JSON-LD block or one hero heading + date/venue. The common
92	  case.
93	- **Listing / index page** — a calendar-of-events or search-results page with many
94	  entries, often an array of `Event` objects or repeated cards. Drives the
95	  multiple-buttons behaviour; the generic fallback can't reliably enumerate these
96	  (it recovers the primary event only — see the fallback-coverage gate).
97	- **Series / recurring page** — one event described as repeating (an `RRULE` in
98	  `.ics`, or schema.org `eventSchedule`). A single page can imply many instances;
99	  how many to surface is genuinely undecided (see Open questions).
100	
101	## Timezone & recurrence semantics
102	
103	- **Timezone** is the trust-critical field: a wrong `ctz` is worse than none —
104	  the unanimity rule, stated in the contract header of
105	  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js` itself (not in the gcec
106	  pack's RULES.md): a zone is returned **only when two independent page-declared
107	  hints agree**, and `""` whenever anything disagrees. The four hint kinds that
108	  file recognises are *stated* (an IANA zone in inline-script JSON), *offset* (the
109	  event's own UTC offset — a trailing `Z` explicitly does **not** count, since
110	  pages habitually serialize in UTC regardless of venue), *country*, and *locale*.
111	  The domain gives three shapes — an
112	  **offset-bearing** instant (ISO-8601 `…+02:00`, or `.ics` `Z`/`TZID`), a
113	  **floating** time (no zone; "same wall-clock everywhere"), and **no time signal
114	  at all**. Only the first lets `ctz` be *derived* rather than guessed.
115	- **Recurrence** (`RRULE`, `eventSchedule`) is currently out of the extension's
116	  scope — it surfaces the event, not its repeat rule. Whether a recurring page
117	  should yield one instance, the next instance, or a note is an open product
118	  question, not a settled requirement. Two 2026 findings narrow *where* the cost
119	  of ever changing that sits:
120	  - **The sink is not the blocker.** Google Calendar's
121	    `render?action=TEMPLATE` link — the exact URL this extension emits — takes an
122	    optional **`recur`** parameter whose value is an RFC-5545 recurrence rule
123	    verbatim: `recur=RRULE:FREQ=DAILY` (`required: no`, `format: text
124	    (RFC-5545 specs)`), and in practice fuller rules such as
125	    `recur=RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;INTERVAL=1;BYDAY=2MO;UNTIL=20250609T000000Z`. So
126	    "hand the user a repeating event" is already expressible in the target we
127	    emit; nothing about the render URL forces the one-instance behaviour.
128	  - **The source side speaks a different vocabulary.** schema.org does *not*
129	    express repeats as an `RRULE` string. A repeating event carries
130	    **`eventSchedule`** → a **`Schedule`**, whose minimum is **`repeatFrequency`
131	    as an ISO-8601 *duration*** (`P1W`, `P1M`, `P1D` — not `FREQ=WEEKLY`),
132	    alongside `byDay` / `byMonth` / `byMonthDay` (e.g. `byDay` as an array of
133	    `https://schema.org/Monday`-style URLs), `scheduleTimezone` (an IANA zone),
134	    `startDate`/`endDate`, `startTime`/`endTime`, and `exceptDate` for
135	    exclusions. Emitting `recur=` from page markup therefore needs a genuine
136	    translation step (`repeatFrequency: P1W` + `byDay` → `FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=…`,
137	    `exceptDate` → `EXDATE`), not a pass-through. **That mapping — plus whether
138	    target sites emit `eventSchedule` at all — is the real cost, not the URL.**
139	  - **And the source signal is absent (measured 2026-08-02): the mapping cost is
140	    moot.** A census of every recorded page in this repo's own extractor corpus
141	    ([`dev/requirements/extractor/data/server-fetched/`](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/tree/main/dev/requirements/extractor/data/server-fetched))
142	    — 36 pages across 24 distinct hosts — finds **zero** occurrences of the
143	    `eventSchedule` property, of `"@type": "Schedule"`, of `repeatFrequency`, and
144	    of any `RRULE` string. (The 15 pages that match a naive `eventSchedule` grep
145	    are all false positives: they carry the *`eventStatus`* enum value
146	    `schema.org/EventScheduled`, an unrelated token.) This is not a rendering
147	    artifact — the pipeline fetches with ScraperAPI `render=true`, so the page's
148	    JS has executed before the snapshot is taken (see
149	    [`scraperapi.mjs`](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/blob/main/.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/create-extractor/scraperapi.mjs)).
150	    So schema.org recurrence is effectively unused across the sites this
151	    extension actually targets, and a `Schedule`→`RRULE` translator would have
152	    nothing to translate. Sampling caveat: hosts enter this corpus because
153	    someone asked for an extractor, which skews toward ticketing/venue *single
154	    instance* pages; a genuinely series-shaped host could still emit it.
155	
156	## Implications for extraction requirements
157	
158	- The format ranking above is *why* the extractor is structured as dedicated
159	  per-site sources + a generic JSON-LD/`og`-first fallback: the machine-readable
160	  layers are the durable signal, the DOM is the last resort.
161	- "An event needs real data, not just a supported host" (gcec pack RULES.md,
162	  *Codebase gotchas*) is a direct consequence of the taxonomy: a host match is
163	  not an `Event` object.
164	- The timezone shapes above are the domain justification for the refusal-to-guess
165	  `ctz` contract — a product-requirements-level stance, distilled in
166	  [`../product-requirements/`](../product-requirements/README.md).
167	- **`Event` JSON-LD is real but a minority signal.** The Google/schema.org usage
168	  statistics (June 2026 dataset) put `schema.org/Event` on **fewer than ~1 million
169	  domains** — an order of magnitude behind common types like `author` (10M+);
170	  Web Data Commons corroborates from the Common Crawl corpus. So a large share of
171	  event pages carry *no* `Event` block, which is exactly why the DOM/text and
172	  `og:`/microdata fallback path (and the fallback-coverage routine) carries real
173	  weight rather than being a rare edge case.
174	- **No dedicated microformats reader is warranted.** The 2026 prevalence check
175	  (see the `h-event` bullet) puts *all* microformats combined under ~1% of pages,
176	  so `h-event`/hCalendar stays a fallback-only concern — extraction effort belongs
177	  on the JSON-LD → Microdata → `og:`/text ladder, not a bespoke hCalendar parser.
178	- **On this project's own target hosts the JSON-LD/fallback split is roughly
179	  60/40 (measured 2026-08-02).** The same corpus census gives the per-target-host
180	  number the web-wide figures could not. Of the **24 distinct hosts** with a
181	  recorded page, **14 carry an `Event`-family JSON-LD `@type`** (bandsintown,
182	  dash.datadoghq.com, dice.fm, eventbrite, eventer.co.il, eventim.co.il,
183	  livenation, luma.com, meetup, seetickets, somo.social, stubhub,
184	  tel-aviv.gov.il, visit.tel-aviv.gov.il). The remaining **10 split in two**:
185	  **5 emit JSON-LD but never an `Event`** (cinema.co.il, comy.co.il, seatgeek,
186	  tabitisrael.co.il, thinkdrink.co.il — typically `Organization`/`WebSite`
187	  boilerplate, which is worse than no JSON-LD because it looks like a hit), and
188	  **5 emit no JSON-LD at all** (barby.co.il, edfringe.com, events.datadoghq.com,
189	  secrettelaviv.com, ticketmaster.co.il). So the DOM/`og:`/text ladder is the
190	  *only* path on ~40% of the hosts this extension supports — the fallback is a
191	  primary code path, not an edge case. Same sampling caveat as above: a host
192	  earns a recorded page by being asked for, and the generic path failing is often
193	  why it was asked for, so this over-samples hard pages relative to the open web.
194	- **`.ics`-only event pages did not appear.** No page in the corpus links a
195	  `.ics` file or serves `text/calendar` in place of in-page markup, so
196	  "follow the download link" is not a fallback worth building on current evidence.
197	
198	## Open questions
199	
200	- ~~A precise `Event`-JSON-LD-vs-fallback split per *target host*.~~ **Answered
201	  2026-08-02** by censusing the recorded extractor corpus: 14 of 24 hosts carry
202	  `Event` JSON-LD, 5 carry JSON-LD without an `Event`, 5 carry none — see the
203	  ~60/40 bullet under Implications. What remains open is narrower: **does the
204	  "JSON-LD but no `Event`" shape (5 of 24 hosts) mislead the generic extractor
205	  into a false positive?** A page with `Organization` JSON-LD and no `Event` is
206	  structurally a fallback case wearing a structured-data costume; the
207	  generic-coverage suite is where that would show.
208	- Recurring/series pages: what's the right product behaviour — one instance, the
209	  next upcoming, or an explicit "this repeats" affordance? (Narrowed 2026-07-26:
210	  the *transport* question is settled — the render URL's `recur=RRULE:…` carries a
211	  repeat rule fine — so this is now purely a product-behaviour choice plus the
212	  `Schedule`→`RRULE` mapping cost, both described above.)
213	- ~~Do any of this extension's target sites actually emit `eventSchedule` /
214	  `Schedule` markup, or is schema.org recurrence effectively unused in the wild?~~
215	  **Answered 2026-08-02: none do** — zero occurrences across 36 recorded pages /
216	  24 hosts (see the recurrence section). The mapping cost identified on 2026-07-26
217	  is therefore not worth paying against today's target set. Worth a re-check only
218	  if a genuinely series-shaped host (a repertory cinema, a weekly class) is added.
219	- ~~Does any meaningful share of target sites express events only via `.ics`
220	  download links (no in-page structured data) worth following?~~ **Answered
221	  2026-08-02: no** — no `.ics` link or `text/calendar` reference in the corpus at all.
222	- **Does JSON-LD-without-an-`Event` cause false positives?** 5 of 24 hosts serve
223	  JSON-LD carrying no `Event` object. Whether the generic extractor treats that as
224	  a structured hit and degrades, or correctly falls through to text, is unmeasured.
225	  Surfaced 2026-08-02.
226	
227	## Sources
228	
229	- [Event — Schema.org Type](https://schema.org/Event)
230	- [Learn About Google Event Schema Markup — Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/event)
231	- [eventAttendanceMode — Schema.org Property](https://schema.org/eventAttendanceMode)
232	- [Microdata vs JSON-LD vs RDFa: Which Structured Data Format to Use in 2026](https://rishikc.com/articles/structured-data-formats-compared-microdata-jsonld-rdfa-2026/)
233	- [microformats.org — microdata](http://microformats.org/wiki/microdata)
234	- [RFC 5545 — Internet Calendaring and Scheduling Core Object Specification (iCalendar)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5545)
235	- [Handling Dates and Times — CalConnect iCalendar dev guide](https://devguide.calconnect.org/iCalendar-Topics/Handling-Dates-and-Times/)
236	- [Announcing the Schema.org usage statistics dataset (blog.schema.org, 2026)](https://blog.schema.org/2026/06/04/announcing-the-schema-org-usage-statistics-dataset/)
237	- [Structured data — 2024 Web Almanac (HTTP Archive)](https://almanac.httparchive.org/en/2024/structured-data)
238	- [Web Data Commons — schema.org data sets](https://webdatacommons.org/structureddata/schemaorg/)
239	- [chimbori/google-calendar-crx — the shut-down "Google Calendar" Chrome extension (archived)](https://github.com/chimbori/google-calendar-crx)
240	- [thanhpd/google-calendar-crx — fork documenting its hCalendar/hResume microformat event detection](https://github.com/thanhpd/google-calendar-crx)
241	- [Microformats — Chrome extension listing (chrome-stats)](https://chrome-stats.com/d/oalbifknmclbnmjlljdemhjjlkmppjjl)
242	- [Google Calendar link parameters (`recur`, `ctz`, `dates`) — add-event-to-calendar-docs](https://github.com/InteractionDesignFoundation/add-event-to-calendar-docs/blob/master/services/google.md)
243	- [RFC 5545 §3.8.5.3 — Recurrence Rule (`RRULE`)](https://icalendar.org/iCalendar-RFC-5545/3-8-5-3-recurrence-rule.html)
244	- [How to Create "Add to Calendar" Links (TeamDynamix KB) — `&recur=RRULE:` example](https://teamdynamix.umich.edu/TDClient/210/DepressionCenter/KB/ArticleDet?ID=13454)
245	- [eventSchedule — Schema.org Property](https://schema.org/eventSchedule)
246	- [Schedule — Schema.org Type](https://schema.org/Schedule)
247	- [Additional `Schedule` type examples — schemaorg/schemaorg Discussion #2948](https://github.com/schemaorg/schemaorg/discussions/2948)
248	- [`dev/requirements/extractor/data/server-fetched/` — this repo's recorded extractor corpus](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/tree/main/dev/requirements/extractor/data/server-fetched) — the 36 pages / 24 hosts censused on 2026-08-02 for `eventSchedule`, `Event` JSON-LD and `.ics` links
249	- [`scraperapi.mjs` — the recording pipeline's `render=true` fetch](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/blob/main/.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/create-extractor/scraperapi.mjs) — why a missing property in the corpus is a real absence, not an unrendered SPA
250	
251	## Growth log
252	
253	- **2026-07-16** — initial seed (folder scaffolding + first research pass on web
254	  event-representation formats, page-shape taxonomy, and timezone/recurrence
255	  semantics).
256	- **2026-07-17** — answered the JSON-LD-prevalence open question directionally:
257	  the Google/schema.org usage stats put `Event` on fewer than ~1M domains (far
258	  behind common types), so `Event` markup is a minority and the DOM/fallback path
259	  carries a large share — added to Implications; narrowed the open question to a
260	  per-target-host measured split via the fallback-coverage corpus.
261	- **2026-07-19** — answered the `h-event`/microformats open question with a real
262	  prevalence check: the HTTP Archive *Web Almanac 2024* puts all microformats
263	  combined below ~1% of pages (vs JSON-LD ~41% / Microdata ~26%), so
264	  hCalendar/`h-event` is a negligible tail not worth a dedicated reader — folded
265	  into the microformats format bullet and Implications; removed that open
266	  question.
267	- **2026-07-26** — worked the recurrence open question and split it in two: the
268	  render URL we already emit accepts `recur=RRULE:…` (RFC-5545, verbatim), so the
269	  sink was never the constraint; schema.org instead models repeats as
270	  `eventSchedule`→`Schedule` with `repeatFrequency` as an ISO-8601 *duration*
271	  (`P1W`) plus `byDay`/`scheduleTimezone`/`exceptDate`, so a real
272	  `Schedule`→`RRULE` translation is where the cost sits. Narrowed the recurrence
273	  question to a pure product-behaviour choice and surfaced a new one (do target
274	  sites emit `eventSchedule` at all). Also corrected two stale repo references
275	  this page carried: `dev/procedures/technicalGotchas.md` no longer exists — its

# Domain

A self-growing wiki of the **problem domain** this extension models: how events
are represented on the web, and how those representations shape what the
extension can extract. Where [`../Market/`](../Market/README.md),
[`../Users/`](../Users/README.md), and
[`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md) cover the outside actors (the
platforms, the people, the rivals), this wiki covers the *thing itself* — the
event data, formats, and page shapes the extractor has to make sense of. It is
the knowledge that most directly drives extraction requirements.

## Key insights

- Not one of the 36 recorded event pages emits schema.org `eventSchedule`, so the recurrence mapping cost is moot.
- `schema.org/Event` sits on under 1M domains, so most event pages carry no Event block at all.
- Of this project's own 24 recorded target hosts, 14 carry Event JSON-LD; the other 10 need DOM, `og:` or text.
- Microformats together are under 1% of pages, so `h-event` never justifies its own parser.
- Google Calendar's render URL already accepts `recur=RRULE:…` — repeats were never blocked by the link we emit.
- A wrong timezone is worse than none, so a zone ships only when two independent page hints agree.
- No recorded target page offers a `.ics` download in place of markup; that page shape does not appear.

## Machine-readable event formats (as of 2026-07-16)

Ordered roughly by how useful they are to a rule-based extractor — highest-signal
first. The project's stance (see the **architecture rules of the road** section of
`.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/RULES.md`, where it reads "prefer extracting
JSON-LD/`og:` (which apps still inject) over brittle DOM positions" — the
`dev/procedures/technicalGotchas.md` this page previously cited was superseded
when that doc was folded into the gcec pack) is to **prefer machine-readable
markup over brittle DOM scraping**, because it survives redesigns and
single-page-app rendering.

- **schema.org `Event` as JSON-LD** — the highest-value target and the one Google
  actively rewards. Emitted as a standalone `<script type="application/ld+json">`
  block, so it is cleanly separable from the page markup and survives client-side
  rendering. Google's required properties are **`name`, `startDate`, and
  `location`**; `startDate`/`endDate` are ISO-8601 **with a UTC/GMT offset**
  (the offset is what lets us derive `ctz` safely — see
  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js`).
  `location` is a `Place` (with `address`: `streetAddress`, `addressLocality`,
  `addressRegion`, `postalCode`) or a `VirtualLocation` (URL only) for online
  events. Since 2020 Google also expects **`eventAttendanceMode`**
  (`Offline`/`Online`/`Mixed`), and as of a June 2025 change requires a **physical
  location** for the rich result at all. Recommended extras that often carry real
  data: `endDate`, `eventStatus`, `image`, `description`, `offers`.
- **Microdata / RDFa** (schema.org vocabulary inline in the HTML) — same
  vocabulary, embedded in the markup rather than a separate block. Common on
  server-rendered sites; JSON-LD is now preferred and gets new features first, so
  microdata/RDFa are a declining but still-present fallback worth reading when no
  JSON-LD block exists. Web-wide, Microdata is still material — the *Web Almanac
  2024* has it steady on roughly a quarter of pages (~26%), well ahead of
  microformats below.
- **`h-event` / hCalendar microformats** — an older, class-attribute convention
  (`h-event`, `p-name`, `dt-start`, `p-location`). Google added hCalendar event
  support back in 2010; adoption has been overtaken by schema.org, but legacy and
  indie-web event pages still use it. **A 2026 prevalence check settles whether
  they're worth a dedicated reader — no:** the HTTP Archive *Web Almanac 2024*
  puts *all* microformats combined below ~1% of pages (hCalendar only a fraction
  of that), against JSON-LD at ~41% (up from 34% in 2022) and Microdata steady at
  ~26%. So `h-event`/hCalendar is a negligible tail; where it does appear, the
  generic text/`og:` fallback is enough. Note: microformats are **not** part of
  the schema.org vocabulary, so any dedicated reader would need its own parser —
  another reason not to build one for a sub-1% format. **Tooling corroboration
  (2026-07-26):** the one browser tool that ever shipped a microformat→calendar
  reader at scale — the Google-encouraged "Google Calendar" Chrome extension,
  which detected `hCalendar` and derivative microformats on the page and offered
  a one-click add — is formally shut down and no longer installable, and the
  generic "Microformats" extension that exported `hCalendar` to iCalendar is
  likewise reported delisted (unmaintained since ~2014). So there is also no
  live microformat event reader left to borrow from (the demand-side reading of
  the same fact is in [`../Competitors/`](../Competitors/README.md)).
- **OpenGraph / meta tags** (`og:title`, `og:description`, and event-ish `<meta>`)
  — not event-specific, but SPA pages very often still inject them, so they are a
  reliable low-fidelity fallback for title/description when nothing structured
  exists.
- **iCalendar (`.ics` / RFC 5545)** — the interchange format calendars import,
  not usually embedded in a page, but the semantic reference for event modelling.
  A `VEVENT` carries `DTSTART`/`DTEND` with a **`TZID`** (or a trailing `Z` for
  UTC, or a bare **floating** time that means "the same wall-clock time in every
  zone"). Recurrence is an **`RRULE`** (`FREQ` = DAILY/WEEKLY/MONTHLY/YEARLY plus
  `INTERVAL`/`COUNT`/`UNTIL`/`BYDAY`…) expanded from `DTSTART`, with `RDATE`/`EXDATE`
  adjustments. This is the vocabulary to match when we reason about timezones and
  repeats even though we target Google Calendar's `render` URL, not `.ics`.

## Page-shape taxonomy

The extractor must first recognise *what kind of event page* it's on — this is the
structural decision behind "one button per event":

- **Single-event page** — one clear event (a concert, a talk, a venue listing).
  Usually one `Event` JSON-LD block or one hero heading + date/venue. The common
  case.
- **Listing / index page** — a calendar-of-events or search-results page with many
  entries, often an array of `Event` objects or repeated cards. Drives the
  multiple-buttons behaviour; the generic fallback can't reliably enumerate these
  (it recovers the primary event only — see the fallback-coverage gate).
- **Series / recurring page** — one event described as repeating (an `RRULE` in
  `.ics`, or schema.org `eventSchedule`). A single page can imply many instances;
  how many to surface is genuinely undecided (see Open questions).

## Timezone & recurrence semantics

- **Timezone** is the trust-critical field: a wrong `ctz` is worse than none —
  the unanimity rule, stated in the contract header of
  `extension/event-extractors/helpers/derive-timezone.js` itself (not in the gcec
  pack's RULES.md): a zone is returned **only when two independent page-declared
  hints agree**, and `""` whenever anything disagrees. The four hint kinds that
  file recognises are *stated* (an IANA zone in inline-script JSON), *offset* (the
  event's own UTC offset — a trailing `Z` explicitly does **not** count, since
  pages habitually serialize in UTC regardless of venue), *country*, and *locale*.
  The domain gives three shapes — an
  **offset-bearing** instant (ISO-8601 `…+02:00`, or `.ics` `Z`/`TZID`), a
  **floating** time (no zone; "same wall-clock everywhere"), and **no time signal
  at all**. Only the first lets `ctz` be *derived* rather than guessed.
- **Recurrence** (`RRULE`, `eventSchedule`) is currently out of the extension's
  scope — it surfaces the event, not its repeat rule. Whether a recurring page
  should yield one instance, the next instance, or a note is an open product
  question, not a settled requirement. Two 2026 findings narrow *where* the cost
  of ever changing that sits:
  - **The sink is not the blocker.** Google Calendar's
    `render?action=TEMPLATE` link — the exact URL this extension emits — takes an
    optional **`recur`** parameter whose value is an RFC-5545 recurrence rule
    verbatim: `recur=RRULE:FREQ=DAILY` (`required: no`, `format: text
    (RFC-5545 specs)`), and in practice fuller rules such as
    `recur=RRULE:FREQ=MONTHLY;INTERVAL=1;BYDAY=2MO;UNTIL=20250609T000000Z`. So
    "hand the user a repeating event" is already expressible in the target we
    emit; nothing about the render URL forces the one-instance behaviour.
  - **The source side speaks a different vocabulary.** schema.org does *not*
    express repeats as an `RRULE` string. A repeating event carries
    **`eventSchedule`** → a **`Schedule`**, whose minimum is **`repeatFrequency`
    as an ISO-8601 *duration*** (`P1W`, `P1M`, `P1D` — not `FREQ=WEEKLY`),
    alongside `byDay` / `byMonth` / `byMonthDay` (e.g. `byDay` as an array of
    `https://schema.org/Monday`-style URLs), `scheduleTimezone` (an IANA zone),
    `startDate`/`endDate`, `startTime`/`endTime`, and `exceptDate` for
    exclusions. Emitting `recur=` from page markup therefore needs a genuine
    translation step (`repeatFrequency: P1W` + `byDay` → `FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=…`,
    `exceptDate` → `EXDATE`), not a pass-through. **That mapping — plus whether
    target sites emit `eventSchedule` at all — is the real cost, not the URL.**
  - **And the source signal is absent (measured 2026-08-02): the mapping cost is
    moot.** A census of every recorded page in this repo's own extractor corpus
    ([`dev/requirements/extractor/data/server-fetched/`](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/tree/main/dev/requirements/extractor/data/server-fetched))
    — 36 pages across 24 distinct hosts — finds **zero** occurrences of the
    `eventSchedule` property, of `"@type": "Schedule"`, of `repeatFrequency`, and
    of any `RRULE` string. (The 15 pages that match a naive `eventSchedule` grep
    are all false positives: they carry the *`eventStatus`* enum value
    `schema.org/EventScheduled`, an unrelated token.) This is not a rendering
    artifact — the pipeline fetches with ScraperAPI `render=true`, so the page's
    JS has executed before the snapshot is taken (see
    [`scraperapi.mjs`](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/blob/main/.claudinite/local/packs/gcec/tasks/create-extractor/scraperapi.mjs)).
    So schema.org recurrence is effectively unused across the sites this
    extension actually targets, and a `Schedule`→`RRULE` translator would have
    nothing to translate. Sampling caveat: hosts enter this corpus because
    someone asked for an extractor, which skews toward ticketing/venue *single
    instance* pages; a genuinely series-shaped host could still emit it.

## Implications for extraction requirements

- The format ranking above is *why* the extractor is structured as dedicated
  per-site sources + a generic JSON-LD/`og`-first fallback: the machine-readable
  layers are the durable signal, the DOM is the last resort.
- "An event needs real data, not just a supported host" (gcec pack RULES.md,
  *Codebase gotchas*) is a direct consequence of the taxonomy: a host match is
  not an `Event` object.
- The timezone shapes above are the domain justification for the refusal-to-guess
  `ctz` contract — a product-requirements-level stance, distilled in
  [`../product-requirements/`](../product-requirements/README.md).
- **`Event` JSON-LD is real but a minority signal.** The Google/schema.org usage
  statistics (June 2026 dataset) put `schema.org/Event` on **fewer than ~1 million
  domains** — an order of magnitude behind common types like `author` (10M+);
  Web Data Commons corroborates from the Common Crawl corpus. So a large share of
  event pages carry *no* `Event` block, which is exactly why the DOM/text and
  `og:`/microdata fallback path (and the fallback-coverage routine) carries real
  weight rather than being a rare edge case.
- **No dedicated microformats reader is warranted.** The 2026 prevalence check
  (see the `h-event` bullet) puts *all* microformats combined under ~1% of pages,
  so `h-event`/hCalendar stays a fallback-only concern — extraction effort belongs
  on the JSON-LD → Microdata → `og:`/text ladder, not a bespoke hCalendar parser.
- **On this project's own target hosts the JSON-LD/fallback split is roughly
  60/40 (measured 2026-08-02).** The same corpus census gives the per-target-host
  number the web-wide figures could not. Of the **24 distinct hosts** with a
  recorded page, **14 carry an `Event`-family JSON-LD `@type`** (bandsintown,
  dash.datadoghq.com, dice.fm, eventbrite, eventer.co.il, eventim.co.il,
  livenation, luma.com, meetup, seetickets, somo.social, stubhub,
  tel-aviv.gov.il, visit.tel-aviv.gov.il). The remaining **10 split in two**:
  **5 emit JSON-LD but never an `Event`** (cinema.co.il, comy.co.il, seatgeek,
  tabitisrael.co.il, thinkdrink.co.il — typically `Organization`/`WebSite`
  boilerplate, which is worse than no JSON-LD because it looks like a hit), and
  **5 emit no JSON-LD at all** (barby.co.il, edfringe.com, events.datadoghq.com,
  secrettelaviv.com, ticketmaster.co.il). So the DOM/`og:`/text ladder is the
  *only* path on ~40% of the hosts this extension supports — the fallback is a
  primary code path, not an edge case. Same sampling caveat as above: a host
  earns a recorded page by being asked for, and the generic path failing is often
  why it was asked for, so this over-samples hard pages relative to the open web.
- **`.ics`-only event pages did not appear.** No page in the corpus links a
  `.ics` file or serves `text/calendar` in place of in-page markup, so
  "follow the download link" is not a fallback worth building on current evidence.
